subject: Neurology
vignette: A 12-year-old boy complains that he cannot read the board at the back of the classroom, although he sees nearby objects clearly. Refraction confirms a refractive error.
question: Which of the following best describes the optical defect and its correction?

options.text: Eye too short; light focuses behind the retina; corrected with a convex lens
Eye too long; light focuses in front of the retina; corrected with a concave lens
Irregular corneal curvature; corrected with a cylindrical lens
Lens opacification; corrected with surgery
Decreased lens elasticity; corrected with reading glasses

explanation_correct: Myopia (nearsightedness) is the most common refractive error and results from an eye that is too long relative to its refractive power, so parallel light rays are focused in front of the retina. It is corrected with concave (diverging) lenses that shift the focal point backward onto the retina. Near objects are seen clearly because diverging rays from near objects focus farther back.

explanation_incorrect.A: A short eye focusing light behind the retina describes hyperopia, which is corrected with convex lenses.
explanation_incorrect.C: Irregular curvature with different refractive power at different axes describes astigmatism, corrected with cylindrical lenses.
explanation_incorrect.D: Lens opacification describes cataract, not a refractive error correctable with glasses.
explanation_incorrect.E: Decreased lens elasticity with age describes presbyopia, which causes impaired near vision.

educationalObjective: Myopia is an elongated eye focusing light in front of the retina and is corrected with concave lenses.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has difficulty seeing close objects clearly and reports that her vision is somewhat clearer at a distance. She is diagnosed with hyperopia.
question: Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of her condition?

options.text: The eye is too long, focusing light in front of the retina
The cornea has irregular curvature, producing different focal lengths in different meridians
The eye is too short, so light would focus behind the retina; a convex lens is used
The lens has become opaque, scattering incoming light
The ciliary muscle is overactive, increasing accommodation

explanation_correct: Hyperopia (farsightedness) results from an eye that is too short for its refractive power, so incoming light would come to focus behind the retina. A convex (converging) lens adds refractive power, moving the focal point forward onto the retina. Unlike presbyopia, hyperopia is due to an axial length/refractive mismatch rather than loss of lens elasticity.

explanation_incorrect.A: An elongated eye focusing light in front of the retina is myopia, corrected with concave lenses.
explanation_incorrect.B: Irregular corneal or lens curvature producing axis-dependent focus is astigmatism, corrected with cylindrical lenses.
explanation_incorrect.D: Opacification of the lens is cataract and causes glare and loss of red reflex, not a simple refractive error.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hyperopia is not caused by overactive accommodation; it is an anatomic refractive mismatch.

educationalObjective: Hyperopia is a short eye focusing light behind the retina and is corrected with convex lenses.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient reports blurred vision at both near and far distances. Refraction reveals that the cornea has unequal curvature in different meridians, giving the eye different refractive power along different axes.
question: Which type of corrective lens is indicated for this condition?

options.text: Cylindrical lens
Concave (diverging) spherical lens
Convex (converging) spherical lens
Prism lens
No corrective lens is effective

explanation_correct: Astigmatism is caused by irregular or asymmetric curvature of the cornea or lens, producing different refractive power at different axes so light cannot be focused to a single point. It is corrected with cylindrical lenses, which have refractive power in one meridian only. Spherical concave and convex lenses correct myopia and hyperopia, respectively.

explanation_incorrect.B: Concave spherical lenses correct myopia by shifting focus backward, not astigmatism.
explanation_incorrect.C: Convex spherical lenses correct hyperopia by adding convergence, not astigmatism.
explanation_incorrect.D: Prism lenses realign images in certain strabismus or diplopia, not to correct astigmatism.
explanation_incorrect.E: Astigmatism is readily corrected with cylindrical lenses or toric contact lenses.

educationalObjective: Astigmatism results from asymmetric corneal/lens curvature and is corrected with cylindrical lenses.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with hyperopia is being fitted for glasses. The optometrist explains that the prescribed convex lenses will improve near vision. The patient asks how adding a converging lens helps when light is already being focused behind the retina.
question: Which of the following best explains why a convex lens improves vision in hyperopia?

options.text: It diverges incoming light so the focal point moves farther back
It increases the axial length of the eye over time
It relaxes the ciliary muscle, flattening the lens
It adds refractive power so light converges sooner and focuses on the retina rather than behind it
It corrects the irregular corneal curvature responsible for the defect

explanation_correct: In hyperopia the eye is too short, so parallel and especially near-divergent light would focus behind the retina. A convex (converging) lens pre-converges incoming rays, increasing the eye's total refractive power so the focal point is shifted forward onto the retinal surface. Concave lenses do the opposite and are used for myopia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Diverging (concave) lenses move the focal point backward and are used for myopia, which would worsen hyperopia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Eyeglasses do not change the anatomic axial length of the eye.
explanation_incorrect.C: Relaxing the ciliary muscle flattens the lens and is not the mechanism by which convex lenses correct hyperopia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Irregular curvature causing axis-dependent focus is astigmatism, which is corrected with cylindrical lenses.

educationalObjective: Convex lenses add refractive power in hyperopia, bringing the focal point forward from behind the retina onto the retina.
